pages.title: About — RegTrac
pages.desc: Scope, method and caveats of RegTrac — the statutory-regulator layer of CashlessConsumer's financial-sector sousveillance stack.
pages.text: About — RegTrac Reg Trac A CashlessConsumer Register Register Timeline Activity Social Blog Search About About What RegTrac tracks, how, and why. Scope RegTrac tracks entities with statutory rule-writing power over India's financial sector: the seven core regulators (RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, IBBI, IFSCA, NABARD), adjacent statutory bodies (DICGC, NHB, SIDBI, NFRA), and non-statutory context entities that shape policy without a statute (FSDC, NPCI). Out of scope by design: self-regulatory organisations — those live in SROTrac. Ministry-level policy making (Department of Economic Affairs, Department of Financial Services, MCA) enters RegTrac only where it touches regulator appointments; the LobbyWatch layer will own it properly. Method The register is a small, auditable CSV — one row per entity — with the statute, establishing date, parent ministry, mandate and consumer grievance route. Leadership rows are added only with an appointment date and a source URL. Claims without a source stay out. The timeline is one row per event, same rule. Everything is regenerated from data by a single build script; the site is static HTML with no trackers, no cookies, no JavaScript dependencies. Caveats Leadership positions are stated as of 12 Sep 2026 and will drift; rows carry their source so the next refresh can re-verify. "Statutory adjacent" bodies (DICGC, NHB, SIDBI, NFRA) are institutions with statutory foundations but narrower or shifted regulatory roles (e.g., HFC regulation moved from NHB to RBI in 2019). FSDC and NPCI are listed as context precisely because they lack statutes — the most consequential coordination in Indian finance happens in a body with no statutory foundation, and the payment rails are run by an industry-owned company. Both facts belong on the record, not in a footnote. The stack RegTrac is layer one of a three-layer sousveillance stack for Indian financial policy making: 1. RegTrac (this site) — the rule-writers : statutory regulators, their powers, appointments, consultations and grievance machinery. 2. SROTrac — the rule-borrowers : RBI-recognised self-regulatory organisations and — the part that matters — their member rosters, where industry consensus on fees and conduct actually forms. 3. LobbyWatch (live at https://lobbywatch.cashlessconsumer.in) — the rule-buyers : who submits on consultations, who meets whom, the revolving door between regulator and regulated, industry-association access to FSDC and ministries. The stack's promise is the join: a consultation submission on an RBI draft (LobbyWatch), cross-referenced against SRO membership (SROTrac), cross-referenced against the regulatory change that followed (RegTrac). Each layer alone is a directory; together they are a map of how financial policy gets made in India — and for whom. Open data `data/regulators.csv`, `data/leadership.csv`, `data/events.csv` and a DuckDB database ship in the repository, plus an `llms.txt` for machine readers. Take it, fork it, build on it — attribution appreciated. Colophon Built by CashlessConsumer — a consumer collective working on digital payments and fintech since 2016. Sister projects: SROTrac , DPI Watch . Corrections: raise an issue on the repository. pages.title: Reserve Bank of India — RegTrac
pages.desc: Reserve Bank of India: statute, powers, leadership, grievance routes and accountability watchpoints — tracked by RegTrac.
pages.text: Reserve Bank of India — RegTrac Reg Trac A CashlessConsumer Register Register Timeline Activity Social Blog Search About ← Register Statutory regulator Reserve Bank of India Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 (operational 1 Apr 1935) Leadership Role Name Since Note Predecessor Src Governor Sanjay Malhotra 2024-12 26th Governor ↗ Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta 2025-04 ↗ Deputy Governor Shirish Chandra Murmu 2025-10 ↗ Deputy Governor T. Rabi Sankar 2021-08 Portfolios: IT, foreign exchange (post-Oct 2025 rejig); in office as of Sep 2026 ↗ Deputy Governor Swaminathan Janakiraman 2023-06 Reappointed 2 years from 26 Jun 2026 (till 2028); portfolios: supervision, financial inclusion ↗ Appointments as of 12 Sep 2026. Sources attached per row. The oldest and most powerful financial regulator in India — and the one that touches the most people. The RBI licenses and supervises banks, NBFCs and payment systems, sets interest-rate policy through the Monetary Policy Committee, and runs the ombudsman scheme that is most Indians' only practical route to compensation when a bank or wallet loses their money. Statute and setup RBI Act, 1934 — the bank began operations on 1 April 1935; nationalised in 1949. Banking Regulation Act, 1949 gives it licensing, supervision and penalty powers over banks. Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 gives it authority over every payment system in India — UPI, cards, wallets, RTGS, NEFT. Central Board: Governor + up to 4 Deputy Governors + government-nominated and regional directors. The Governor is appointed by the Centre (Appointments Committee of the Cabinet) — there is no independent selection process. What it regulates Scheduled commercial banks, small finance banks, payments banks, RRBs, cooperative banks (banking side) NBFCs, housing finance companies (since Aug 2019, taken from NHB) Payment system operators and intermediaries — including NPCI (UPI, RuPay, AePS), wallet issuers, payment aggregators Credit information companies; asset reconstruction companies; money lenders through state partnership Exchange rate and forex (FEMA, 1999, jointly with the Centre) Powers that matter Issue, suspend and cancel licences; impose moratoria (the Yes Bank moratorium, 2020, is the template) Monetary policy: statutory inflation target of 4% (+/- 2%) under the 2016 amendments; MPC rate decisions Directions and master directions — the real rulebook; everything from UPI transaction limits to NBFC conduct Recognition of self-regulatory organisations: the SRO-FT framework (draft Jan 2024) produced FACE (Aug 2024) and UFF (Sep 2026) — tracked in SROTrac Depositor protection lever: ₹5 lakh deposit insurance via DICGC (a wholly owned subsidiary) Leadership (as of 12 Sep 2026 — see leadership table; Governor: Sanjay Malhotra since Dec 2024; Deputy Governors appointed by the Centre: Poonam Gupta (Apr 2025), Shirish Chandra Murmu (Oct 2025).) For the person paying Grievance route: complain to your bank/wallet first; if no reply in 30 days or you are unsatisfied, escalate free to the RBI Integrated Ombudsman — cms.rbi.org.in. Zero-MDR on UPI and debit cards is a statutory mandate (from Jan 2020) — if a merchant refuses UPI or adds a "UPI charge", that is a violation, not a policy. Unclaimed deposits sit in RBI's Depositor Education and Awareness fund — the RBI runs drives to return them; check your family's dormant accounts. Watchpoints (capture and accountability) The top jobs are central-government appointments; the Board mix is government-nominated. Leadership churn (2024-25) happened entirely through ACC decisions. The SRO framework formally hands industry consensus formation (fees, codes, grievance standards) to industry bodies — SROTrac tracks who those members are . Consultation practice: draft master directions invite comments, but the RBI does not systematically publish who commented or what changed — the LobbyWatch gap. Sources RBI Act, 1934 / BR Act / PSS Act (RBI leg

pages.title: Securities and Exchange Board of India — RegTrac
pages.desc: Securities and Exchange Board of India: statute, powers, leadership, grievance routes and accountability watchpoints — tracked by RegTrac.
pages.text: Securities and Exchange Board of India — RegTrac Reg Trac A CashlessConsumer Register Register Timeline Activity Social Blog Search About ← Register Statutory regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India SEBI Act, 1992 (statutory; existed as non-statutory body since 1988) Leadership Role Name Since Note Predecessor Src Chairperson Tuhin Kanta Pandey 2025-02 Madhabi Puri Buch ↗ Whole-Time Member Sandip Pradhan 2025-12 ↗ Whole-Time Member Kamlesh Chandra Varshney 2023-09 Reappointed 2026-09-15 by ACC (DoPT order; gazette S.O. 5142(E), 18 Sep) beyond 19 Sep 2026 until 4 Aug 2029 or further orders; oversees Corporate Finance, CFI, Integrated Surveillance, Legal Affairs ↗ Whole-Time Member Amarjeet Singh 2023-09 3-year term ended Sep 2026; renewal not announced as of 2026-10-02 — flagged for checking ↗ Whole-Time Member K V Ramana Murty 2026-04 3-year term; took charge 15 Apr 2026 (PR 24/2026); IDAS (1991) officer, ex-Addl CGDA ↗ Appointments as of 12 Sep 2026. Sources attached per row. The markets regulator. Everything listed, everything pooled, everything sold as an investment: brokers, mutual funds, AIFs, IPOs, takeover codes, insider trading. SEBI writes the rules, licenses the players, investigates, and adjudicates — all three powers in one body, which is both its strength and its standing conflict-of-interest. Statute and setup Set up in 1988 as a non-statutory body; given teeth by the SEBI Act, 1992 after the Harshad Mehta securities scam. Quasi-legislative (regulations), quasi-executive (investigation) and quasi-judicial (orders) powers in one institution. Board: Chairperson + Whole-Time Members + RBI Deputy Governor + ministry joint secretary + part-time members. Chair and WTMs are central-government appointments. What it regulates Stock brokers, depositories, exchanges and clearing corporations Mutual funds, AIFs, PMS, portfolio managers, investment advisers and research analysts Listed companies (LODR), takeovers, insider trading, buybacks and delisting Foreign portfolio investors; credit rating agencies; debenture trustees; online bond platforms Powers that matter Search, seizure, summons, disgorgement, settlement without admission; market-wide bans on bad actors T+1 settlement made India the first large market to run it (Jan 2023); optional T+0 beta since 2024 Disclosure regimes it keeps re-tightening after every episode of promoter abuse Leadership (as of 12 Sep 2026 — Chairperson: Tuhin Kanta Pandey since Feb 2025, succeeding Madhabi Puri Buch; Whole-Time Member Sandip Pradhan inducted Dec 2025. Pandey told Reuters in Mar 2026 he had spent his first year in 77 meetings with foreign investors, easing entry rules.) For the person paying Grievance route: SCORES 2.0 — scores.gov.in — mandatory online escalation for everything from broker payout delays to mutual fund NAV disputes; SMART ODR offers online conciliation and arbitration. SEBI's own studies have repeatedly found most retail F&O traders lose money — Reuters reported the pattern again in Mar 2026. The regulator knows the house odds and says so; the products are still on sale. Check adviser/broker registration on SEBI's site before paying anyone for "stock tips". Watchpoints (capture and accountability) The previous chair's 2024-25 term ended amid unprecedented public scrutiny of the chair's personal disclosures — the appointment process itself (ACC, no public shortlist) was the structural weakness everyone pointed at. Consultation papers are public; who responds, and which responses get accepted, is not systematically published — the LobbyWatch gap. Industry-standard setters (AMFI, BASL, ANMI) are SEBI-recognised SROs — industry writing its own code again; their rosters are a future SROTrac extension. pages.text: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India — RegTrac Reg Trac A CashlessConsumer Register Register Timeline Activity Social Blog Search About ← Register Statutory regulator Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India IRDA Act, 1999 Leadership Role Name Since Note Predecessor Src Chairperson Ajay Seth 2025-07-24 Former DEA Secretary Debasish Panda ↗ Whole-Time Member (Life) Swaminathan S Iyer 2025 ↗ Appointments as of 12 Sep 2026. Sources attached per row. The policyholder's regulator — in theory. IRDAI licenses insurers and intermediaries, approves products, and sits on top of grievance machinery (Bima Bharosa, insurance ombudsmen) that handles hundreds of thousands of complaints a year, dominated by mis-selling and claim rejections. Statute and setup IRDA Act, 1999 ended LIC/GIC's monopoly and created the regulator; constituted 2000. Headquarters: Hyderabad. Board: Chairperson + Whole-Time Members, appointed by the Centre. What it regulates Life, general and health insurers (state-owned and private, 60+) Intermediaries: agents, brokers, web aggregators, TPAs, insurance marketing firms Reinsurance arrangements, including the GIFT City reinsurance pathway (with IFSCA) Powers that matter Product approval — now shifting to a "use and file" regime for many categories, which speeds launch and moves consumer risk from pre-approval to post-hoc enforcement Licensing and penalties for mis-selling and claim-delay violations Policyholder protection regulations: disclosure, claim timelines, health claim charters (2024, with the General Insurance Council) Leadership (as of 12 Sep 2026 — Chairperson: Ajay Seth since 24 Jul 2025, succeeding Debasish Panda; Whole-Time Member for Life: Swaminathan S Iyer (2025).) For the person paying Grievance route: Bima Bharosa portal (IRDAI) escalates insurer complaints; the Insurance Ombudsman (cioins.gov.in, 15 offices) awards compensation free of cost. Claim rejection or delay: ombudsman first, court later. Mis-selling of ULIPs and traditional plans by bank "relationship managers" is the classic case — the commission structure rewards it; ask for the benefit illustration and surrender value in writing before signing. A claim must be repudiated or paid within statutory timelines; delay itself is compensable. Watchpoints (capture and accountability) The 2023-25 reform wave ("Insurance for All by 2047", use-and-file, FDI liberalisation announced in the 2025 Budget and legislated that year) loosens pre-market checks; consumer protection has to be won in enforcement instead. Industry bodies (GI Council, Life Council, IBAI) co-write charters and standard terms — whose draft wins is not published. Insurer-side data: grievance volumes by insurer are published; enforcement actions against insurers for repeat grievance patterns are not — the asymmetry that lets bad claims behaviour persist. pages.title: Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority — RegTrac
pages.desc: Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority: statute, powers, leadership, grievance routes and accountability watchpoints — tracked by RegTrac.
pages.text: Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority — RegTrac Reg Trac A CashlessConsumer Register Register Timeline Activity Social Blog Search About ← Register Statutory regulator Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority PFRDA Act, 2013 (statutory w.e.f. 1 Feb 2014; interim body since 2003) Leadership Role Name Since Note Predecessor Src Chairperson Sivasubramanian Ramann 2025-06-20 Former Deputy CAG and CTO Office of CAG ↗ Appointments as of 12 Sep 2026. Sources attached per row. The youngest of the big-four regulators. PFRDA runs the National Pension System and Atal Pension Yojana — the retirement money of government employees, since 2004, and any citizen who opts in. Its core consumer problem: subscribers take all the market risk, while fund managers take management fees on other people's retirement. Statute and setup Created by executive order in 2003; made statutory by the PFRDA Act, 2013 (w.e.f. 1 Feb 2014). Chairperson + members, appointed by the Centre. What it regulates Pension fund managers under NPS (public and private schemes) and APY Central recordkeeping agencies (CRAs: Protean, KFin) — where your PRAN actually lives Points of presence (banks etc.) that onboard subscribers; retirement advisers The NPS Trust structure, through which the assets are held Powers that matter Registration and penalty powers over pension funds, CRAs and PoPs Investment-pattern regulations — how much of your money goes to equity, corporate debt, government paper, AIFs Subscriber-protection regulations (2022): exit norms, service standards, withdrawal timelines Scheme design: the 2025 assured-payout and inflation-indexed NPS products were shaped through expert panels the chairperson convenes Leadership (as of 12 Sep 2026 — Chairperson: Sivasubramanian Ramann, assumed charge 20 Jun 2025; former Deputy CAG. In office, PFRDA has pushed mobile/UPI onboarding for informal workers and set up a panel on assured 10-year payout options under NPS.) For the person paying Grievance route: NPS Ombudsman (PFRDA Redressal of Subscriber Grievance Regulations, 2015) after CRA/PoP escalation; APY subscribers ride on bank grievance machinery too. Fund-manager choice matters less than tier and scheme choice: the government default scheme exists for people who do not want to pick. At exit, annuity purchase is mandatory for a large share of the corpus — annuity pricing is set by insurers regulated by IRDAI, not PFRDA. Your pension regulator does not control your pension payout. Watchpoints (capture and accountability) Pension funds are subsidiaries of the same fund houses and insurers whose products they "compete" on — fee and default-scheme design are the places to watch. Product design by expert panel (assured payout, inflation-linked NPS) is good process, but panel composition and submissions are not published. Coverage push toward informal workers via UPI-based micro-contributions will make PFRDA a mass-market DPI regulator — consumer protection staffing has not visibly scaled to match. pages.title: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India — RegTrac
pages.desc: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India: statute, powers, leadership, grievance routes and accountability watchpoints — tracked by RegTrac.
pages.text: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India — RegTrac Reg Trac A CashlessConsumer Register Register Timeline Activity Social Blog Search About ← Register Statutory regulator Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (Board constituted 1 Oct 2016) Leadership Role Name Since Note Predecessor Src Chairperson Ravi Mital 2021-10 Still in office as of Sep 2026 (gazette signatures May 2026; NCLAT order 8 Sep 2026); succession search opened Jun 2026 M S Sahoo ↗ Appointments as of 12 Sep 2026. Sources attached per row. The regulator for the end of the corporate life cycle: insolvency professionals, their agencies, information utilities, and the process rules under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. For consumers it matters disproportionately — homebuyers became financial creditors under the IBC, so IBBI process rules decide whether flat-buyers in a stuck project recover money or watch it dissipate. Statute and setup Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (enacted May 2016); IBBI constituted 1 October 2016. Chairperson + members appointed by the Centre through a government-run selection process. What it regulates Insolvency professionals (registration, code of conduct, disciplinary action) Insolvency professional agencies (ICSI, ICAI, ICMAI arms — SROs by another name) Information utilities — the credit-record layer that proves default Process regulations: CIRP, liquidation, individual insolvency (under-used) Powers that matter Rule-making for the entire CIRP/liquidation pipeline; the 2026 amendment run (liquidation fourth amendment; CIRP fourth amendment in Jun 2026) kept rewriting committee-of-creditors and cost rules Suspension and de-registration of professionals Grievance handling: Grievance and Complaint Handling Regulations, amended Feb 2026 Leadership (as of 12 Sep 2026 — Chairperson: Ravi Mital, appointed 2021, still in office — signing gazette notifications in May 2026 and referenced in an NCLAT order of 8 Sep 2026 — while the government opened the search for his successor in Jun 2026, ahead of schedule. Succession to these posts is where accountability attaches; the early-start search process itself is worth watching for transparency of shortlists.) For the person paying Grievance route: IBBI's complaint system (regulations amended Feb 2026) — against insolvency professionals and agencies; homebuyer claims inside CIRP go through the resolution professional and NCLT, not IBBI directly. If your builder is in CIRP: file your claim with the RP on time, keep the allotment proof; IBBI rules decide voting and recovery mechanics, but the clock is unforgiving. Outcomes are poor and slowing: corporate resolutions hit a 13-quarter low in early 2026 (36 cases resolved in the quarter, per Times of India reporting) — the statutory outer limit of 330 days is routinely overshot. Watchpoints (capture and accountability) The regulator enforces the profession it oversees through committee structures that courts keep constraining: in Jul 2026 the Calcutta High Court held the Chairperson cannot act as the Disciplinary Committee under the IBC. Structural separation of prosecution and adjudication inside IBBI is unfinished business. The IBC Amendment Act, 2026 bars resolution professionals from acting as liquidators in the same matter — a revolving-door fix forced by persistent practice. The Corporate Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026 (Clause 73) would make IBBI the country's statutory valuation authority — a major power expansion grafted onto an insolvency regulator; valuation is where insolvency money is made and lost. Committee-of-creditors discretion (CoC is dominated by financial creditors) is where consumer claims get haircuts; IBBI writes those rules. Sources Business Today: IBBI opens search for next Chairperson (Jun 2026) IBC Laws: Liquidation Process (Fourth Amendment) Regulations, 2026 — signed RAVI MITAL, Chairperson NCLAT order referencing Ravi Mital as Chairperson (8 Sep 2026) LiveLaw: C

pages.title: International Financial Services Centres Authority — RegTrac
pages.desc: International Financial Services Centres Authority: statute, powers, leadership, grievance routes and accountability watchpoints — tracked by RegTrac.
pages.text: International Financial Services Centres Authority — RegTrac Reg Trac A CashlessConsumer Register Register Timeline Activity Social Blog Search About ← Register Statutory regulator International Financial Services Centres Authority IFSCA Act, 2019 (operational 1 Oct 2020) Leadership Role Name Since Note Predecessor Src Chairperson K. Rajaraman 2023-09 Tenure extended to Oct 2028 (Aug 2026) Injeti Srinivas ↗ Appointments as of 12 Sep 2026. Sources attached per row. India's youngest and most unusual regulator: one authority, all sectors, one square kilometre. Since 1 October 2020, IFSCA has replaced RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA inside GIFT City — banking, markets, insurance, pensions, fintech — with a mandate to compete with Singapore and Dubai. Speed is the product; the governance question is whether speed is being regulated. Statute and setup IFSCA Act, 2019 (enacted Dec 2019); operational 1 Oct 2020. Chairperson + members appointed by the Centre. Chairperson K. Rajaraman's tenure was extended to Oct 2028 in Aug 2026. What it regulates IFSC Banking Units (56+ banks), capital-market intermediaries, insurance and reinsurance entities (GIFT Re), aircraft and ship leasing, fintech sandbox participants Offshore-rupee products, GIFT-listed securities, diaspora retail products as they open up Within the IFSC, IFSCA rules displace the sectoral regulators' rulebooks entirely Powers that matter Unified single-window regulation — every licence, every rule, one body Regulatory sandbox with forbearance powers (relaxations from Indian financial rules inside the zone) Cross-regulator negotiation: IFSCA asks SEBI/MoF for enabling changes when its products collide with the mainland perimeter — e.g., the May 2026 SEBI consultation to let online bond platforms distribute IFSC-regulated overseas debt Leadership (as of 12 Sep 2026 — Chairperson: K. Rajaraman since Sep 2023, tenure extended till Oct 2028 (Aug 2026); predecessor: Injeti Srinivas, the founding chair.) For the person paying Mostly business-to-business today, but the pipeline — GIFT-domiciled "Global Indian" accounts, retail diaspora investment products — is aimed at individual savers. When IFSC retail products reach you, your grievance route will be IFSCA's, not RBI's or SEBI's. Watch deposit insurance: IFSC products sit outside DICGC's domestic cover. "Guaranteed" in an IFSC brochure has a different legal meaning. Watchpoints (capture and accountability) One regulator writing banking + markets + insurance rules at speed, with sandbox forbearance and limited parliamentary scrutiny of IFSC rulebooks — the thinnest accountability-to-power ratio in Indian financial regulation. Boundary bargaining with mainland regulators (bond platforms, reinsurance) happens in consultation papers that read technical but reallocate entire product categories. Leadership extension (2026) with no published selection benchmark — consistent with the ACC-appointment pattern across all regulators. pages.title: National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development — RegTrac
pages.desc: National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development: statute, powers, leadership, grievance routes and accountability watchpoints — tracked by RegTrac.
pages.text: National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development — RegTrac Reg Trac A CashlessConsumer Register Register Timeline Activity Social Blog Search About ← Register Statutory regulator National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development NABARD Act, 1981 (established 12 Jul 1982) Leadership Role Name Since Note Predecessor Src Chairman Shaji K V 2022-12 Confirmed in office as of Sep 2026 ↗ Appointments as of 12 Sep 2026. Sources attached per row. Part development bank, part supervisor. NABARD refinances rural credit and runs India's farm-infrastructure funds — and, less visibly, carries statutory supervisory duties over cooperative banks and regional rural banks, the weakest links in India's deposit-safety chain. Statute and setup NABARD Act, 1981 ; established 12 July 1982 on the B. Sivaraman Committee recommendation, taking over RBI's rural credit functions. Chairman + directors; the RBI holds a stake and the Centre controls appointments. What it regulates (supervises) Statutory inspection of state cooperative banks, central cooperative banks and regional rural banks (Banking Regulation Act powers as applicable to them) Rural infrastructure funding (RIDF), micro-finance ecosystem funds, climate and agri-innovation stacks (e.g., DiCRA with UNDP) Not a conduct regulator: farmers and depositors of co-op banks are served (or failed) through the institutions NABARD supervises, but consumer grievances route to the RBI ombudsman Powers that matter Refinance volumes as credit steering — NABARD decides which lending models get cheap money Supervisory findings that feed RBI action on weak cooperative banks Fund administration for most central-sector rural schemes — budget execution power without budget visibility Leadership (as of 12 Sep 2026 — Chairman: Shaji K V, in office since Dec 2022, confirmed in office as of Sep 2026.) For the person paying If you bank with a cooperative bank, your deposit insurance comes from DICGC like anyone else's, but supervision is split between NABARD and RBI — when co-op banks fail, both blame the arrangement. RIDF and NABARD-funded infrastructure is public money; project lists are published but outcomes rarely are. Watchpoints (capture and accountability) Cooperative banking supervision is the longest-running accountability muddle in Indian finance — NABARD inspects, RBI licenses, state registrars co-exist; failures (the urban co-op pattern) fall between chairs. Appointment and tenure norms for the chairman track the PSU-bank pattern (Centre-decided) rather than an independent process.
